Stork B.lab_name: Molecular Biology of Cellular Stress Responses group, Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Medical Faculty and University Hospital Düsseldorf, Heinrich Heine University (Düsseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Stork B.role: Heisenberg Professor for the molecular biology of cellular stress responses at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, who studies the ULK1 complex, the switch that starts autophagy, and how it is wired to the energy sensor AMPK and to mTOR
Stork B.sub: Heisenberg Professor (W2), Molecular Biology of Cellular Stress Responses, Medical Faculty, Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (since 2017) · Group leader, Institute of Molecular Medicine I, Düsseldorf (2011–2017) · Junior group leader, University of Tübingen (2006–2011) · PhD, Bielefeld, Göttingen and Kansai Medical University, Osaka (2002–2006)
story: Autophagy, the cell's self-digestion system, is started by a protein kinase called ULK1. When energy runs low, the energy sensor AMPK switches ULK1 on, and when nutrients are plentiful mTORC1 switches it off. In LOF2011, from Björn Stork's group, then at the University of Tübingen, Antje Löffler and colleagues found that the signal also runs backwards: ULK1 adds phosphate groups to AMPK and dampens its activity. This makes a negative feedback loop, a built-in way for the autophagy machinery to limit the signal that started it, rather than a one-way switch. The work was done in cell and biochemical experiments.

Stork studied biochemistry in Bielefeld, with a semester at McGill University in Montreal, and did a PhD in biochemistry and molecular immunology from 2002 to 2006 under J. Wienands and T. Kurosaki, with the work split between Bielefeld, Göttingen and Kansai Medical University in Osaka. From 2006 to 2011 Stork led a junior research group at the University of Tübingen, where LOF2011 was done, and then moved to the Institute of Molecular Medicine I at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf as a group leader, completing the habilitation (the German qualification to teach and supervise at university level) in molecular medicine there in 2013. In 2015 the team mapped the short stretch of the protein ATG13 that holds ULK1 in place and found that cells lacking this contact still keep some autophagy, which points to routes that bypass the usual ULK1-ATG13 link.

Since 2017 Stork has held a Heisenberg Professorship, a German research council post for established researchers, for the molecular biology of cellular stress responses at the Düsseldorf medical faculty. The group's central theme is how signals switch autophagy on and off, with the longer-term aim of using autophagy control in cancer, infection and nerve development. In 2026, as senior author, Stork reported that human induced pluripotent stem cells and nerve progenitor cells have working autophagy machinery but do not switch it on after low-dose DNA damage, unlike many cancer cell lines.
sources: PubMed search Stork B[Author] AND (autophagy OR ULK1) AND Düsseldorf, 33 results

Birsoy K.lab_name: Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, The Rockefeller University (New York, New York, USA)
Birsoy K.role: Cancer metabolism researcher who trained with Jeffrey Friedman and David Sabatini and now heads the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics at The Rockefeller University, using genetic screens to find how cancer cells rewire their metabolism
Birsoy K.sub: Associate Professor and head of the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, The Rockefeller University (title as of 2023) · Postdoc, David Sabatini laboratory, Whitehead Institute and MIT (papers 2012–2015) · PhD, The Rockefeller University, Jeffrey Friedman laboratory
story: Kivanç Birsoy is a co-author of two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute. The 2012 Nature paper (YIL2012) showed in mice that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells, the cells that sit next to intestinal stem cells and support them. With less mTORC1, Paneth cells send signals that make the neighbouring stem cells more numerous and more active. The 2014 Cancer Discovery paper (GRA2014) went through MTOR mutations found in human cancers, identified 33 that switch the pathway on, and showed that cancer cells carrying them were more sensitive to rapamycin in cell culture and in mouse tumour grafts. That suggests the mutations could help pick patients who might respond to mTOR inhibitors.

Birsoy did a PhD at The Rockefeller University in the laboratory of Jeffrey Friedman, the discoverer of the fat hormone leptin, and then joined David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute as a postdoctoral fellow. Birsoy's own first-author work there was on cell metabolism. A 2015 Cell paper used a CRISPR screen to find genes that cells need when their mitochondria are blocked by the drug phenformin. It showed that one essential job of the mitochondrial electron transport chain in dividing cells is to let them make the amino acid aspartate, and that cells without a working chain can grow if they get extra aspartate.

Birsoy returned to Rockefeller to lead the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, and a 2023 profile lists the title as associate professor. The lab studies how cancer cells reprogram metabolic pathways, especially oxidative metabolism, using unbiased genetic screens together with large-scale measurements of metabolites and proteins. A 2026 paper in Cell Chemical Biology, for example, used CRISPR screens to identify TXNDC15 as a missing part of the system that removes faulty proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, with effects on lipid balance.
Birsoy K.note: PhD (Rockefeller, Friedman lab), postdoc (Sabatini) and Associate Professor title from a 2023 UMass Chan MetNet interview profile, not a Rockefeller page; title may since have changed (check rockefeller.edu). Source spells the name Kivanc; kept Kivanç. PhD year not found.

Perez K.role: Aging researcher and co-founder of the Swiss company EPITERNA, working with Alejandro Ocampo's lab at the University of Lausanne on screening platforms that look for drugs extending lifespan across several species
Perez K.sub: Co-founder, EPITERNA SA, Épalinges · Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of Lausanne, Ocampo lab (papers 2023–2026)
story: Many drugs extend lifespan in one lab animal and then fail in the next. Kevin Perez is first author of a 2026 paper describing a platform built to tackle that problem (PEREZ2026). It tests compounds in yeast, nematode worms, fruit flies, killifish and mice, uses automated imaging and a deep-learning program to spot when each animal dies, and has screened more than 400 compounds under thousands of conditions. By comparing species, it picks out compounds that work in several of them and shows that hits tend to act on known conserved longevity pathways, mTOR among them. The paper is about methods and infrastructure; individual hits still need checking in mammals and eventually people.

Perez is a co-founder of EPITERNA, a start-up set up with Alejandro Ocampo, who leads an aging lab at the University of Lausanne and is the company's CEO. The company aims to develop affordable products that slow aging and delay age-related disease. PubMed lists Perez with both EPITERNA SA and the Ocampo group in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the University of Lausanne. Earlier work includes a 2023 first-author study showing that mouse models of premature aging with defects in DNA repair have an older 'epigenetic age', measured from DNA methylation, than their real age, unlike other premature aging models, and a 2025 study in which a two-chemical reprogramming cocktail reduced signs of aging in human cells and extended lifespan in worms.
Perez K.note: Co-founder role from a Forever Healthy (Rejuvenation Startup Summit 2024) speaker announcement, not a company page. Location changed to canonical "Épalinges, Switzerland". Training not found.

Sillito F.lab_name: Chakraverty Lab, UCL Cancer Institute, University College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Sillito F.role: Haematologist at the Royal Marsden Hospital and University College London with a special interest in CAR-T cell therapy and lymphoma, whose PhD showed that forcing mTORC1 on in CD4+ T cells makes them last longer but tire out
Sillito F.sub: Haematologist with a special interest in cellular therapy and high-grade lymphoma, Royal Marsden Hospital and University College London Hospitals (2025–2026) · PhD, UCL Cancer Institute, MRC Clinical Research Fellow (completed 2023) · Specialist haematology training, University College London Hospitals · Medical degree, University College London (2009)
story: Cancer treatments with engineered T cells, such as CAR-T and TCR-T cells, work only if the infused cells survive and keep fighting. In a 2026 Journal of Immunology paper, with Ronjon Chakraverty as senior author, Francesca Sillito made mouse CD4+ helper T cells produce extra RHEB, a protein that switches on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. After transfer into mice the cells first grew more and lasted longer, but over time they became exhausted: they carried brake-like receptors on their surface and divided poorly when they met their target again. CD8+ killer T cells had been reported to react differently to the same change. The study is in mice and warns that boosting mTORC1 in therapeutic T cells has a cost.

Sillito is a haematologist, a doctor who treats blood diseases and blood cancers. Sillito graduated in medicine from University College London in 2009 and completed specialist haematology training at University College London Hospitals; an early case report from 2011 lists Sillito at Basildon University Hospital. With a Medical Research Council clinical research fellowship, Sillito then did a PhD on T-cell therapies at the UCL Cancer Institute, completed in 2023, working with Ronjon Chakraverty and Hans Stauss; with Angelika Holler and Stauss, Sillito wrote a 2020 review on engineering CD4+ T cells to strengthen cancer immunity. The 2026 paper above comes from that work.

Sillito now works at the Royal Marsden Hospital with a special interest in cellular therapy, including CAR-T, and high-grade lymphoma, and is a principal investigator on several cellular therapy and lymphoma trials. As first author in Haematologica (2025), Sillito studied how blood stem-cell clones change after CAR-T therapy and the risk of later myeloid cancers, and has co-authored UK studies of second-line CAR-T treatment for large B-cell lymphoma from University College London Hospitals and the Royal Marsden Hospital.
